title: Medication Documentation and High-Alert Awareness

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe accurate medication documentation.
- Explain high-alert medication awareness.
- Recognize when to clarify or report medication discrepancies.
- Apply look-alike/sound-alike safeguards in medication documentation.
- Follow scope-of-practice when escalating medication concerns to licensed staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a recipe card. To bake correctly you need the ingredients and amounts and steps. A medication note is the same — it needs the medicine name, how much, how it is taken, and how often.

### Question 2

Imagine your chore list and your family's copy of it don't match. Reconciliation is sitting down together and making sure both lists say the same thing so nothing important is missed.

### Question 3

The route is just the 'how' — like whether you eat a snack or rub lotion on your skin.

### Question 4

Frequency answers the question 'how many times a day?' — like brushing your teeth twice a day.

### Question 5

If a recipe's amount is smudged, you wouldn't guess how much flour — you'd ask the person who wrote it. Same idea here: ask, don't guess.

### Question 6

A tiny dot is easy to miss. Putting a '0' in front of it is like putting a bright flag on the dot so nobody walks past it.

### Question 7

Half a milligram is written '0.5' — always put a '0' before the dot and never add an extra '0' after the 5.

### Question 8

The MAR is like a checklist where every time a medicine is due and given, someone writes it down so everyone knows exactly what happened and when.

### Question 9

If you know a food might make you sick but can't remember how, you'd still warn people — and you'd say 'I'm not sure exactly what happens.'

### Question 10

Even 'natural' or store-bought items can mix badly with medicines, so the care team needs the full picture of everything the patient takes.

### Question 11

When you fix a mistake in an important notebook, you cross it out with one line and write the fix next to it, and sign it — never scribble it out completely.

### Question 12

You can't write down that you did your homework before you actually did it — the record has to match what really happened.

### Question 13

If you can't remember a song's name, you'd look it up — you wouldn't write down 'the one that goes la-la-la.' Same for medicines: get the real name.

### Question 14

A prescription is the note from the doctor that says exactly which medicine the pharmacy should give the patient.

### Question 15

It's like writing both a person's nickname and their real name so everyone knows you mean the same person.

### Question 16

Medicines go in their own special folder in the chart so the whole team can always find the up-to-date list in one place.

### Question 17

Like repeating a phone number back to the person on the line to make sure you wrote it right — say the whole order back and check.

### Question 18

A sloppy little 'u' can look like a '0,' so writing the whole word 'units' keeps the number safe.

### Question 19

If a friend stopped taking their medicine, you wouldn't secretly change their chart or order them to restart — you'd tell the grown-up in charge and write down what they said.

### Question 20

Writing the date and time is like putting a timestamp on a text message — it shows exactly when something happened.

### Question 21

Copying a list is like copying homework — check every line against the original so nothing gets changed by accident.

### Question 22

Knowing what a person is allergic to is just as important as knowing what medicine they take, so it gets written down right beside the medicine list.

### Question 23

It's like writing both 'bike' and 'bicycle' on a list of what you own — you don't own two things, it's the same thing twice.

### Question 24

If the teacher's homework instructions don't say how many pages or when it's due, you ask the teacher — you don't just make it up.

### Question 25

A cup of strong coffee and a cup of weak coffee look the same, but one has more caffeine — writing down the strength tells you what's really in the cup.

### Question 26

Some medicines are like very sharp tools — they work great when used exactly right, but if used wrong they can hurt badly. Those are the 'handle with care' medicines.

### Question 27

Insulin is a very powerful helper for people with diabetes, but getting the amount wrong can make their blood sugar drop too low, which is dangerous.

### Question 28

Blood thinners are medicines that make blood less 'sticky' so it doesn't clot — but too much can cause bad bleeding, so they need extra care.

### Question 29

Strong pain medicines can help a lot, but too much can make a person's breathing slow way down, so they must be watched carefully.

### Question 30

One word is about how dangerous a mistake would be; the other is about how often something happens. They're two different ideas.

### Question 31

Insulin brings blood sugar down. Give a little too much and sugar can fall too low, which can make a person very sick very fast.

### Question 32

These medicines make blood less likely to clot, which is helpful — but too much means a small cut could bleed a lot, so the amount has to be just right.

### Question 33

Strong pain medicines can make a person's breathing get very slow and shallow if they get too much — that's why they're 'handle with care.'

### Question 34

Potassium is a salt the body needs, but a big concentrated dose can stop the heart's rhythm — so it has to be handled with extreme care.

### Question 35

Cancer medicines are very strong — they attack fast-growing cells, so getting the dose wrong can hurt the body in serious ways.

### Question 36

Two sets of eyes catch more mistakes than one — like having a friend re-check your math before you turn it in.

### Question 37

Dangerous or easy-to-mix-up items get their own special shelf and a bright label so nobody grabs the wrong one by accident.

### Question 38

Out of that list, the insulin is the one where a small mistake could hurt the most, so it gets the most careful look.

### Question 39

The assistant is the careful note-taker and the messenger who raises a flag — the doctors and nurses are the ones who make the medicine decisions.

### Question 40

If you almost tripped on a loose rug, you'd tell someone so it could be fixed — you wouldn't wait for someone to actually fall.

### Question 41

Insulin is counted in special 'units,' not in teaspoons or milliliters, so a note saying 'mL' is a warning sign that someone should check again.

### Question 42

There are safety experts whose whole job is figuring out which medicines are the trickiest, and they publish the list so clinics know what to watch.

### Question 43

For the 'handle with care' medicines, you check the name and amount twice, like measuring twice before you cut.

### Question 44

When someone asks 'how much medicine should I take,' the assistant passes that question to the doctor — the assistant never guesses at doses.

### Question 45

If you found something dangerous sitting where it shouldn't be, you'd tell an adult in charge instead of hiding it or throwing it away yourself.

### Question 46

A mistake in the medicine process is one thing; harm from a medicine is another. They often overlap, but they are not the same thing.

### Question 47

If you don't understand a shorthand word in important instructions, you ask the person who wrote it — you don't guess what it means.

### Question 48

It's not about how popular a medicine is — it's about how much trouble a mix-up could cause.

### Question 49

When two things look almost the same, you make them look different on purpose — big labels, special shelves — so no one grabs the wrong one.

### Question 50

Some medicines make muscles go completely limp, including the ones you breathe with — those are extremely 'handle with care.'

### Question 51

Some medicine names are like 'cat' and 'hat' — they look and sound almost the same, so it's easy to mix them up.

### Question 52

If you grab the wrong medicine because its name sounds like another, someone could take the wrong pill — that's the danger.

### Question 53

When two words look almost the same, you make the different letters BIG so people see the part that's different.

### Question 54

Write the whole name in clear print — like making sure your handwriting is neat so the teacher doesn't misread 'cat' as 'hat.'

### Question 55

Having two names for the same thing is like having a person's first and last name — if you mishear one, the other helps you get it right.

### Question 56

If two names look almost the same, go back and check the original note or ask — don't just pick one.

### Question 57

Like spelling your name over the phone so the other person writes it right — repeat and spell it back to be sure.

### Question 58

If two boxes look identical, you put them on different shelves so you don't accidentally grab the wrong one.

### Question 59

It's like a slippery floor next to a staircase — each risk is bad alone, but together they make a much bigger danger.

### Question 60

If two names differ by just one letter, that's a clue to double-check — like noticing 'dog' and 'dig' and making sure which word was meant.

### Question 61

Your brain can flip two almost-identical words without you noticing, so it's safer to look at the real note than to rely on 'I think I remember.'

### Question 62

If you think someone got the wrong medicine, you tell the person in charge right away — you don't wait and you don't hide it.

### Question 63

It's not just names — two medicine boxes can look almost identical too, and that can also cause a mix-up.

### Question 64

If you shorten two similar words, the short versions can look even more alike — like 'app' and 'ape.'

### Question 65

Slow down and check twice — that's the secret to not grabbing the wrong thing when two names look alike.

### Question 66

If you can't read a note, you ask the person who wrote it — you never fill in a guess.

### Question 67

If the instructions don't say how many times a day, you ask for the missing piece instead of making one up.

### Question 68

Like repeating a phone number back to make sure you wrote it down right — you say it back and check.

### Question 69

If the list and the patient's story don't match, you tell the person in charge so they can sort it out — you don't just change things on your own.

### Question 70

You fix a mistake by adding a clearly labeled 'whoops, corrected on this date' note — you don't pretend the mistake never happened.

### Question 71

When something about a medicine doesn't look right, you tell your supervisor — the person whose job it is to fix it — not just anyone.

### Question 72

When something goes wrong, you write down what happened so everyone can learn how to keep it from happening again.

### Question 73

If a number looks way too big, you ask 'is this right?' before writing it down — you don't quietly change it.

### Question 74

If you spill something, you tell a grown-up and clean it up properly — you don't pretend it didn't happen.

### Question 75

If the patient says 'I also take this,' you write it down and tell the care team — you don't pretend it doesn't matter.

### Question 76

Check the name, the amount, the way it's taken, and who it's for — like checking a package before you label it.

### Question 77

When someone asks a tricky medicine question, the assistant passes it to the expert instead of guessing an answer.

### Question 78

If you can't tell which medicine someone means, ask them to read the label or check with the doctor — don't guess.

### Question 79

The assistant can raise the alarm and write things down, but they can't change the doctor's order — that's the doctor's job.

### Question 80

If two notes disagree, you don't pick one or split the difference — you ask the person in charge which is right.

### Question 81

A 'near miss' is like almost tripping on a loose step — telling someone lets them fix the step before anyone actually falls.

### Question 82

If you're not sure how to spell a word, you look it up before writing it — especially when it's a medicine name.

### Question 83

The assistant gathers the facts and passes them to the expert — they don't decide the answer themselves.

### Question 84

Write down just the facts — what you saw and who you told — like a reporter, not a detective.

### Question 85

If someone uses a shortcut that the rules say not to use, you ask them to write it out the safe way instead.

### Question 86

Before writing anything down, check the 'five rights': the right person, medicine, amount, way of taking it, and timing.

### Question 87

If the note doesn't say how the medicine is taken, ask — don't just guess 'by mouth.'

### Question 88

If the medicine on the order is one the patient is allergic to, you shout 'stop!' and tell the doctor — you never just write it down.

### Question 89

If a number could be 1 or 10, you ask which one it is — you never pick or average them.

### Question 90

Writing down 'I told Nurse Smith at 2:00' is like leaving a note that proves the important message was passed on and received.
